summaries.example: Imagine a true sentence: “There is a hidden red marble in the box, but nobody knows it.” If someone knew this whole sentence, they would know that nobody knows about the marble. But then at least one person would know about it after all. This strange sentence seems impossible to know. Fitch’s idea is that if every truth could possibly be known, even this sentence would have to be knowable. That creates a contradiction.
summaries.summary: Fitch’s paradox examines a tempting idea: every true statement could be known by someone at some possible time. The argument also starts with the ordinary thought that some truths are not known yet. It then considers a special truth of the form, “This is true, but nobody knows it.” If that whole truth could be known, the knower would know both the truth and that nobody knows it. That seems to make the sentence impossible to know. The argument therefore appears to turn “every truth is knowable” into the much stronger claim that every truth is already known. Philosophers have suggested several responses. Some revise the logic used in the argument. Others distinguish different kinds of situations or meanings of “possible,” or limit the knowability rule to certain statements. The SEP entry explains the argument and the continuing debate about whether any proposed response succeeds.
key_ideas: The puzzle begins with the thought that every truth can possibly be known.
It also assumes that some truths are not known right now.
A carefully chosen sentence says that it is true but unknown. Knowing that whole sentence would make it no longer unknown.
Philosophers disagree about whether the argument shows that all truths cannot be knowable or whether some part of the reasoning should be changed.
Proposed replies change the logic, the meaning of knowability, or the kinds of statements to which the rule applies.
summaries.why_it_matters: The paradox tests the connection between truth and knowledge. It asks whether saying that truth can be discovered is really different from saying that all truths are already known. The issue matters in theories about meaning, science, mathematics, and how inquiry can reach truth. It also shows how a very simple-looking rule can have unexpected results when it is applied to a sentence that talks about knowledge itself.

important_terms.definition: A statement or claim that matches the facts.
Having the right information that a statement is true.
The idea that any true statement could be known by someone, sometime, even if it is not known now.
A puzzle in reasoning where starting assumptions lead to a surprising or seemingly impossible result.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be true even when nobody knows it?
Would knowing “nobody knows this” change what is known?
Is a rule still useful if applying it to itself causes trouble?
Which seems more reasonable: that every truth is knowable, or that some truths may be unknowable?

summaries.example: Let p mean “There is an unknown truth about a distant planet.” Consider the compound claim p and “p is not known.” If that compound is true, the knowability principle says it could be known. Yet knowledge of the compound would include knowledge of p and knowledge that p is not known. Since knowledge is normally taken to imply truth, the latter knowledge would make p known, contradicting the compound’s second part. The argument does not merely show that this particular claim is hard to discover; it is used to derive that no truth can be unknown if every truth is knowable.
summaries.summary: Fitch’s paradox concerns theories that connect truth with possible verification or knowledge. The knowability principle says that every true proposition is possibly known. The argument also uses the existence of an unknown truth. Substituting the proposition “p is true and p is not known” into the principle yields possible knowledge of that compound. But if the compound were known, ordinary principles about knowledge would yield both knowledge of p and the truth that p is not known. Since knowledge is factive, the compound cannot be known. Thus the premises produce a contradiction, and the principle appears to imply that every truth is actually known. The result threatens a middle position between realism, on which some truths may be unknowable in principle, and a naive idealism that identifies truth with what is known. The SEP entry surveys attempts to diagnose or block the result. Intuitionistic logic rejects some classical inferences but faces problems involving non-omniscience and undecided statements. Paraconsistent logic questions whether contradictions must be impossible. Semantic proposals distinguish knowing in a situation from knowing about a situation, while modal proposals restrict substitution to rigid expressions. Syntactic proposals apply knowability only to selected statements. None is presented as an uncontested final solution; the source emphasizes that there is no consensus about exactly where the proof fails, if it fails at all.
key_ideas: The formal core is KP: for every proposition p, p implies that it is possibly known. Combined with an unknown truth, KP can be applied to the proposition that is true but unknown.
Knowledge of a conjunction is normally taken to include knowledge of each conjunct, and knowledge entails truth. These modest assumptions make the relevant conjunction impossible to know.
The classical argument reaches actual omniscience: if all truths are knowable, then all truths are known. The paradox is the apparent collapse of moderate epistemic anti-realism into naive idealism.

Intuitionistic revisions block some classical steps, such as moving from the negation of a negation to the original claim. But they may still yield troubling consequences, including claims about unknown or undecided statements.
Paraconsistent proposals allow some contradictions without allowing every conclusion, though they must explain which modal inferences the Fitch proof uses.

Restriction strategies modify KP by limiting its quantifier, using situations, rigid reference, or syntactic classes such as Cartesian or basic statements. The entry reports objections and Fitch-like arguments against several restrictions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The paradox is a compact test case for theories of truth, meaning, knowledge, and modality. It shows that “discoverable in principle” may be stronger than it first appears when the principle ranges over propositions that describe their own epistemic status. It also illustrates a general philosophical method: examine which logical rules, semantic assumptions, and forms of quantification support an argument. The proposed replies clarify important distinctions—actual versus possible knowledge, rigid versus non-rigid reference, classical versus nonclassical logic, and unrestricted versus restricted principles—even when they do not settle the debate.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that for every proposition p, if p is true, then it is possible for p to be known.
A proposition is factive when knowing it entails that it is true; the SEP argument treats knowledge as factive.
The claim that some truth is not actually known, either by an individual or collectively.
A modal operator meaning that something is possible; in the entry, its interpretation is central to the debate.
A logic that does not accept every classical inference, especially unrestricted removal of double negation.
A logic in which contradictions need not make every statement follow; contradictions do not automatically trivialize the theory.
An expression whose reference remains fixed across possible circumstances, unlike a non-rigid expression.
A proposal that limits knowability to statements with a particular logical form or proof-theoretic property.

questions_to_think_about: Does the paradox refute the unrestricted knowability principle, or does it expose an invalid assumption about knowledge, possibility, or substitution?
Is “not every truth is known” a satisfactory expression of non-omniscience in intuitionistic logic if it is not equivalent to “some truth is unknown”?
Should a theory of truth be revised to avoid self-referential or epistemically complex propositions?
What independent reason could justify restricting the knowability principle rather than merely blocking the paradox?
Does allowing true contradictions clarify the problem, or does it create a different explanatory burden?

summaries.example: Suppose a school has a true but unknown fact: “The missing library key is in one of the lockers, and nobody knows which locker.” Call this whole statement S. If S is knowable, someone could learn S. But learning S would mean learning both that the key is in a locker and that nobody knows which locker. That person would then know something about the key, so the “nobody knows” part would no longer be correct. The example models Fitch’s move: a truth that includes its own unknownness seems unable to become known.
summaries.summary: Fitch’s paradox begins with a plausible-sounding principle: every truth is knowable, at least in some possible circumstance. It also considers the ordinary fact that people do not know every truth. From an unknown truth p, Fitch forms the more complicated statement “p is true and p is not known.” If this statement is true, the knowability principle says that it could be known. However, knowing the whole statement would include knowing p and knowing that p is not known. Because knowledge normally entails truth, this would make p known and unknown at once. The argument therefore appears to show that universal knowability leads to universal actual knowledge. This creates a problem for moderate forms of anti-realism, which aim to connect truth with possible verification while still allowing that we are not omniscient. The SEP entry describes several responses. Intuitionists reject some classical inferences and may express non-omniscience as “not all truths are known,” rather than as “some truth is unknown.” Paraconsistent theorists question whether contradictions must destroy a theory. Semantic proposals distinguish the situation where knowledge occurs from the situation the knowledge concerns. Other proposals restrict the knowability principle to certain kinds of statements. The source presents these as debated approaches, not as an agreed solution.
key_ideas: Fitch’s proof combines universal knowability with the weaker, commonsense idea that at least one truth is currently unknown.
The crucial substitution uses a statement that says both that p is true and that p is not known. The statement is apparently true but cannot itself be known.
The surprising conclusion is not simply that some facts are difficult to learn. It is that universal knowability entails universal actual knowledge.
Some philosophers treat this as a refutation of verificationist or anti-realist theories; others see it as a paradox because the collapse seems too quick.
Intuitionistic logic avoids one classical step, but the source notes further difficulties involving undecided statements and claims such as “if p is unknown, p is false.”
Other responses change the meaning of knowledge or possibility, allow contradictions without triviality, or restrict which statements count as knowable.
summaries.why_it_matters: This paradox helps explain why philosophers distinguish truth, knowledge, possibility, and verification instead of treating them as interchangeable. It also demonstrates how the exact wording and logical form of a statement can matter. A theory may seem sensible when discussing ordinary facts but encounter trouble when it is applied to a statement about its own knowability. Studying the proposed repairs gives a useful introduction to debates about realism, nonclassical logic, and the limits of philosophical principles.

important_terms.definition: The claim that if a statement is true, then there is some possible time or situation in which someone knows it.
A statement that is true but not known by anyone at the relevant time or in the relevant group.
The philosophical view that truth is connected to what could be verified, proved, or known, rather than being wholly independent of inquiry.
The view that some truths may remain unknowable even in principle and are not made true by what people can know.
A logical rule saying that knowing “A and B” involves knowing A and knowing B.
The idea that knowledge requires truth: if someone knows A, then A is true.
A logic that keeps some classical rules, such as rejecting unrestricted double-negation elimination, because truth may be tied to construction or proof.
A strategy that prevents the paradox by allowing the knowability rule to cover only selected propositions.

questions_to_think_about: Is the statement “p is true but unknown” a legitimate substitution into a rule about every truth?
Could a theory reasonably reject the idea that knowledge of a conjunction includes knowledge of both parts?
Why might an anti-realist prefer intuitionistic logic even apart from this paradox?
When does limiting a general principle become a principled clarification rather than an ad hoc escape?
Does the paradox concern human limits, logical impossibility, or both?
